spans.text: The man who swapped hats
Almost nobody remembers how this novel ends, and it ends by taking itself away.

A nameless man attends high mass in the cathedral on the Hradschin, picks up the wrong hat from the pew, goes back to his hotel and sleeps for one hour. In that hour he lives another man’s entire life: thirty years of it, a murder trial, a love affair, a woman he never meets again, the destruction of a city quarter. He wakes, reads the name in the hatband, and spends the rest of the book trying to find out whether Athanasius Pernath was ever real.
The answer he gets is not yes and not no. It is a gilded gate on the Hradschin, a house that nobody can enter, and his own face looking back at him.

Readers who come to The Golem expecting a monster story find instead a book about a man wearing another man’s head, and this is not a trick played at the end. It is the whole design. Pernath spends the novel failing to remember who he is, and the reader spends it inside a borrowed skull. The hat is the novel’s thesis, and Meyrink puts it on the first page he can and takes it off on the last.
A banker in a cell

Gustav Meyrink was born Gustav Meyer in Vienna on 19 January 1868, the illegitimate son of a Württemberg government minister, Baron Karl von Varnbüler, and an actress, Maria Wilhelmina Adelheid Meier. He grew up as the son of nobody in particular, and he never lost the outsider’s eye for how respectable people close ranks.

In 1888 he helped found a bank in Prague. In 1891 he came through a personal crisis that turned him towards the occult for the rest of his life: Theosophy, the Kabbalah, Freemasonry, yoga, alchemy. He was a founding member of a Theosophical lodge. This was not a literary pose adopted later to furnish a novel. It came first, by more than twenty years.
Then in 1902 he was accused of fraud, spent two months in prison, and came out with his banking career destroyed. He was not convicted. The accusation was enough.

This matters to the book you are holding more than any of the occultism does. The prison chapters of The Golem are the best writing in it, and they are not imagined. The sausage broth salted with soda, the clock face with no hands, the examining magistrate who bares his teeth before he speaks, the bleating clerk behind the second desk, the president of the court who draws a revolver when a prisoner steps towards him: a man who has only read about prison does not know which details to keep. Meyrink knew, and the knowledge cost him everything he had.
The Golem is not the monster
Anybody who has met the Golem anywhere else will meet a different creature here.

The familiar story is this: in the reign of Rudolf II, the great Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague made a man out of clay, animated him with a written name placed in his mouth, used him as a servant, forgot one Friday to remove the name, and had to unmake him when he ran wild. Zwakh tells that version in Chapter Four, accurately, as a thing people say.

It is worth knowing that the legend is younger than it sounds. The attachment of the Golem to Rabbi Loew is a nineteenth century development, not a medieval one, and its near canonical form was printed by Leopold Weisel in 1847 in Sippurim, an anthology of Bohemian Jewish tales published in Prague by Wolf Pascheles. Meyrink’s readers knew that book the way English readers know Grimm.
And Meyrink does almost nothing with it.

His Golem is not made of clay and has no master. It appears in the Jewish quarter about every thirty three years, walks a little way, and vanishes. It is beardless, yellow faced, with slanting eyes, and it moves as though it is always about to fall forward. It does no work and obeys nobody. Zwakh, who has thought about it for a lifetime, offers the only explanation the book endorses: that it is a psychic epidemic, the soul of the quarter itself accumulating like electrical charge until it discharges in the shape of a man. Hillel goes further and suggests it is a thought, thought so hard by a medieval rabbi that it became able to return without him.
Which means that when the Golem finally walks into the novel and sits down, it is wearing Pernath’s face.

That is the book’s real subject: not a monster made by a man, but a man who discovers he may himself be the made thing. The Kabbalistic term for the double, Habal Garmin, the breath of the bones, is given to us early and quietly by Hillel, and everything afterwards is its working out. The room in the Altschulgasse that has no door and only a barred window, where the Golem is supposed to live, is described by Hillel in almost the same words as the human soul.
A city being demolished while he wrote it
The ghetto in this book was being destroyed as it was written, and Meyrink knew it.

The Prague slum clearance, the asanace, was sanctioned by the Emperor Franz Joseph in February 1893. Demolition began in 1895 and the bulk of it was finished by 1914. More than a hundred and twenty buildings came down. The medieval lanes were replaced by apartment blocks and the wide new boulevard of Pařížská; the old synagogues and the cemetery survived only because they had been declared monuments.

The Golem was serialised in the magazine Die Weißen Blätter from December 1913 to August 1914, precisely as the last of it was going. So when Pernath comes out of prison at the end of the novel and finds the Hahnpassgasse a field of rubble, with workmen digging by torchlight and the exposed rooms of his own house hanging in the air like cells of a honeycomb, that is not a symbol Meyrink invented. It is reportage, and it is an elegy.

The book was an enormous success. It sold something in the order of two hundred thousand copies in its first year in print, 1915, which is a strange and rather terrible fate for a novel about a place that had just been demolished, published into the first year of a war.
What holds it together

Readers sometimes complain that the plot of The Golem is loose. It is, if you read it as a thriller about a blackmailing junk dealer. It is not loose at all if you notice that the book is built on a single Kabbalistic idea and keeps restating it.

The idea is given a name in Chapter Two: Ibbur, the impregnation of the soul. A book is brought to Pernath by a stranger with no memorable face, and the chapter where he reads it is the chapter in which his old life ends. From then on there are two ways in front of him, and Hillel names them: the way of life and the way of death. Pernath is told he has already chosen and has forgotten choosing.

Everything else rhymes with that. Charousek chooses hatred and follows it with a purity that the book plainly calls holy. Laponder, the lust murderer, has taken the other path and goes to the gallows as to a wedding. Mirjam waits for a miracle and will not be robbed of it. Wassertrum cannot choose at all and is destroyed by a thing he could not stop wanting. When the headless figure offers Pernath the grains and he strikes them out of its hand, he is refusing the choice itself, and he is told later that this was a third way nobody expected.

And at the end, in the garden on the Hradschin, the gate is a hermaphrodite: the male half and the female half forming the two leaves of a door, which is what Mirjam said she was waiting for, and what Laponder said was the key he had been missing.
The novel is not a mess. It is a set of variations, and the theme is stated in the second chapter.
A word on the dark
It should be said plainly, since this edition is meant to be honest with its readers, that The Golem contains passages about the Jewish inhabitants of the ghetto, and one passage in particular about
“stocks”
and
“blood”

, that a reader in the twenty first century will find ugly. They are given to characters, chiefly to Charousek, whose whole psychology is a hatred of inherited blood and who is himself the son of the man he hates. Meyrink was not writing propaganda and was later banned by the regime that did. But the ugliness is in the book and it is not glossed over here, because an edition that quietly smoothed it away would be lying about what 1915 sounded like.
What is also in the book, and is rarer, is Schemajah Hillel: the poorest man in the quarter, the only one Wassertrum does not dare approach, and the still point the entire novel turns on.

Six hundred and seventy words, and the entire novel is in them. A man half asleep, a sentence from a life of the Buddha about a crow and a stone that looks like a lump of fat, and a voice that will not stop asking about that stone. Note that the dreamer here is not Pernath. He is the man from the last chapter, and he has just fallen asleep in a hotel wearing somebody else’s hat. Note also the waning moon failing on its left side, which is astronomically impossible and is discussed in the note on the translation.
The moonlight falls on the foot of my bed and lies there like a large, pale, flat stone.

When the full moon begins to shrink in its shape, and its left side starts to fail, the way a face going towards old age shows its first lines on one cheek and grows thin, then at that hour of the night a dull, tormenting restlessness takes hold of me.

I am not asleep and I am not awake, and in the half dream what I have lived mixes in my soul with what I have read and what I have heard, the way currents of different colour and clearness flow together.
I had been reading about the life of the Buddha Gotama before I lay down, and in a thousand variations one passage went through my mind, beginning again from the start each time:

A crow flew down to a stone that looked like a lump of fat, and thought: perhaps there is something good to eat here. And when the crow found nothing good to eat there, it flew away. Like the crow that approached the stone, so do we, we the tempters, abandon the ascetic Gotama, having lost our pleasure in him.
And the image of the stone that looked like a lump of fat grows monstrous in my brain:
I walk along a dried out riverbed and pick up smooth pebbles.

Grey blue ones with glittering dust sprinkled through them, which I brood over and brood over and can still make nothing of; then black ones with sulphur yellow markings, like a child’s attempts to model clumsy speckled newts, turned to stone.
And I want to throw these pebbles far away from me, but they keep falling out of my hand, and I cannot banish them from my sight.
All those stones that ever played a part in my life rise up around me.

Some labour heavily to work their way up out of the sand into the light, like big slate coloured crabs when the tide comes back, as though they would stop at nothing to draw my eyes to them, to tell me things of infinite importance.
Others, exhausted, fall back powerless into their holes and give up ever getting a word in.

Now and then I start up out of the twilight of these half dreams and see for a moment the moonlight lying again on the bunched foot of my blanket like a large, pale, flat stone, only to grope blindly after my fading consciousness once more, searching restlessly for that stone which torments me, which must lie hidden somewhere in the rubble of my memory and looks like a lump of fat.

A rainwater pipe must once have emptied onto the ground beside it, I imagine, bent at an obtuse angle, its edges eaten away with rust, and stubbornly I try to force such a picture on my mind, to lie to my startled thoughts and lull them to sleep.
I do not succeed.

Again and again, with an absurd persistence, a wilful voice inside me insists, tireless as a shutter that the wind knocks against the wall at regular intervals: that it is quite otherwise, that this is not the stone that looks like fat at all.
And there is no getting free of the voice.

If I object a hundred times that all of it is quite beside the point, it falls silent for a little while, then wakes again unnoticed and begins stubbornly once more: good, good, quite so, but still it is not the stone that looks like a lump of fat.
Slowly an unbearable feeling of helplessness begins to take hold of me.
How things went on from there I do not know. Did I give up all resistance of my own accord, or did they overpower me and gag me, my thoughts?
I know only that my body lies sleeping in the bed, and that my senses are cut loose and no longer bound to it.
Who is

now, I want to ask suddenly, and then I remember that I no longer possess any organ with which I could ask a question; and then I am afraid that the stupid voice will wake again and begin the endless interrogation about the stone and the fat all over.
And so I turn away.

The dream closes over and Pernath’s Prague begins. Meyrink introduces almost the entire cast in one chapter: Aaron Wassertrum the junk dealer, red Rosina, the twins Loisa and Jaromir, Zwakh the puppeteer, and the woman who bursts in with a gold brocade over her bare shoulders. The passage about the
“stocks”

in the ghetto is the ugliest thing in the book; it is Pernath thinking, not Meyrink lecturing, and it is left as written. Watch the last two pages, where the name in the hatband surfaces for the first time.

Suddenly I was standing in a gloomy courtyard, looking through a reddish archway across the narrow, filthy street at a Jewish junk dealer leaning against a vaulted shopfront that was hung about its edges with old scrap iron, broken tools, rusted stirrups and skates and a great many other dead things.

And this picture had about it the tormenting monotony that marks all those impressions which cross the threshold of our perception day after day, so many times over, like pedlars, and it roused in me neither curiosity nor surprise.
I became aware that I had been at home in these surroundings for a long time.
This feeling too left me no deeper impression, for all that it contradicted what I had perceived only a moment before and the question of how I had come here.

I must at some time have heard or read a strange comparison between a stone and a lump of fat, the thought forced itself on me as I climbed the worn steps to my room and reflected in passing on the greasy look of the stone thresholds.

Then I heard footsteps running on ahead of me up the stairs above, and when I reached my door I saw that they had belonged to Rosina, the fourteen year old red haired girl of the junk dealer Aaron Wassertrum.
I had to pass close by her, and she stood with her back against the banister and bent herself lasciviously backwards.
She had laid her dirty hands around the iron rail to steady herself, and I saw how her bare forearms shone out pale from the murky half dark.
I avoided her eyes.
Her insistent smile disgusted me, and that waxen rocking horse face.
She must have spongy white flesh like the axolotl I saw earlier in the salamander cage at the bird dealer’s, I felt.
The eyelashes of red haired people are as repellent to me as a rabbit’s.
And I unlocked my door and slammed it quickly shut behind me.
From my window I could see the junk dealer Aaron Wassertrum standing in front of his shop.
He was leaning in the entrance of the dark arch, picking at his fingernails with a pair of pincers.
Was the red haired Rosina his daughter or his niece? He bore no resemblance to her.

Among the Jewish faces I see surfacing day after day in the Hahnpassgasse I can plainly distinguish several separate stocks, which the close blood relation of individuals blurs as little as oil will mix with water. There one may not say: those two are brothers, or father and son.
This one belongs to that stock and this to another, and that is all the features will tell you.
And what would it prove even if Rosina did look like the junk dealer!

These stocks nurse a secret loathing and revulsion for one another that breaks through even the barriers of close kinship, but they know how to keep it hidden from the outside world as one guards a dangerous secret.

Not one of them lets it show, and in this agreement they are like hate filled blind men clinging to a filthy rope: one with both fists, another only reluctantly with a finger, but all of them possessed by a superstitious fear that they must be lost the moment they let go of the common hold and separate themselves from the rest.
Rosina belongs to the stock whose red haired type is more repulsive still than the others. Whose men are narrow chested and have long chicken necks with protruding Adam’s apples.

Everything about them seems freckled, and their whole lives long these men suffer torments of lust, waging a secret, unbroken, unsuccessful war against their own appetites, tortured by a perpetual and sickening anxiety about their health.
I was not clear how I came to connect Rosina with the junk dealer Wassertrum at all.
I had never seen her anywhere near the old man, nor noticed that the two of them had ever called out a word to each other.
She was also almost always in our courtyard, or lurking about the dark corners and passages of our house.
Certainly all my fellow tenants take her for a near relation of the dealer, or at least his ward, and yet I am convinced that not one of them could give a reason for the supposition.
I wanted to tear my thoughts away from Rosina, and looked down from the open window of my room into the Hahnpassgasse.
As though Aaron Wassertrum had felt my glance, he suddenly turned his face up towards me.
His rigid, hideous face with the round fish eyes and the gaping upper lip split by a harelip.
He seemed to me like a human spider, one that feels the faintest touch on its web however indifferent it pretends to be.
And what can he live on? What does he think about, and what is he planning?
I did not know.
On the edges of the wall around his shop hang the same dead worthless things, unchanged, day after day and year in year out.

I could have drawn them with my eyes shut: here the bent tin trumpet with no keys, the yellowed picture painted on paper with its strangely assorted soldiers. Then a garland of rusted spurs on a mouldering leather strap, and other half rotted rubbish.
And in front, on the ground, stacked close together so that nobody can cross the threshold of the shop, a row of round iron stove plates.
None of these things ever grew in number or diminished, and if now and then a passer by really did stop and ask the price of one thing or another, the dealer would fly into a violent agitation.

He would draw up his lip with the harelip in a way that made the blood run cold, and splutter out something unintelligible in a gurgling, stumbling bass, until the buyer lost all desire to ask further and went on his way, put off.
Aaron Wassertrum’s glance had slid from my eyes with the speed of lightning, and now rested with close interest on the bare walls that join my window from the house next door.
What could he possibly see there?
The house stands with its back to the Hahnpassgasse and its windows look into the courtyard. Only one is turned to the street.

By chance the rooms next door on the same floor as mine, which I believe belong to an oddly angled studio, seemed to have been entered at that moment, for through the wall I suddenly heard a man’s voice and a woman’s talking together.
But the dealer could not possibly have noticed that from below.
Someone moved outside my door, and I guessed: it is still Rosina, standing out there in the dark in greedy expectation that I might after all call her in to me.

And below, half a storey down, the pockmarked, half grown Loisa lies in wait on the stairs with held breath to see whether I will open the door, and I can positively feel the breath of his hatred and his foaming jealousy reaching up to me.
He is afraid to come closer and be noticed by Rosina. He knows himself dependent on her as a hungry wolf on its keeper, and would like nothing better than to leap up and give his fury its head.
I sat down at my work table and looked out my tweezers and gravers.
But I could get nothing done, and my hand was not steady enough to repair the fine Japanese engravings.
The dull, gloomy life that clings to this house will not let my mind come to rest, and old pictures keep rising in me.
Loisa and his twin brother Jaromir are hardly a year older than Rosina.
Their father, who had been a baker of communion wafers, I could scarcely remember any longer, and now an old woman looks after them, I believe.
Only I did not know which one she was among the many who live hidden in the house like toads in their holes.
She looks after the two boys, that is to say: she gives them shelter, and for that they must hand over to her whatever they occasionally steal or beg.
Does she give them anything to eat as well? I could not think it, for the old woman only comes home late in the evening.
She is said to be a washer of corpses.
Loisa, Jaromir and Rosina I often saw playing together harmlessly in the courtyard as children.
But that time is long past.
All day now Loisa is after the red haired Jewish girl.
Sometimes he hunts for her a long while in vain, and when he can find her nowhere he creeps up to my door and waits with a contorted face for her to come here in secret.
Then, as I sit at my work, I see him in my mind’s eye out there lurking in the crooked passage, his head with its wasted neck bent forward, listening.
Sometimes a wild noise suddenly breaks through the silence.

Jaromir, who is deaf and dumb, and whose every thought is filled with one unbroken insane craving for Rosina, roams the house like a wild animal, and the inarticulate howling bark he sets up, half out of his senses with jealousy and suspicion, sounds so ghastly that it stops the blood in your veins.

He hunts for the pair of them, whom he always supposes to be together, hidden somewhere in one of the thousand filthy holes, in a blind frenzy, forever whipped by the thought that he must stay at his brother’s heels so that nothing can happen with Rosina that he does not know of.
And it is precisely this ceaseless torment of the cripple, I suspected, that is the stimulant driving Rosina to take up with the other one again and again.
If her inclination or her willingness weakens, Loisa thinks up some fresh abomination to kindle Rosina’s appetite anew.

Then they let themselves be caught by the deaf mute, in appearance or in fact, and lure the raving creature treacherously after them into dark passages, where they have built vicious traps out of rusty barrel hoops that spring up when they are trodden on, and iron rakes with the points turned upward, into which he must fall and cut himself bloody.
From time to time Rosina, to stretch the torture to its utmost, devises something hellish on her own account.
Then she changes her behaviour towards Jaromir at a stroke and acts as though she had suddenly taken a liking to him.

With her everlasting smile she communicates things to the cripple in haste that throw him into an almost insane excitement, and she has invented for this a sign language that seems full of mystery and is only half comprehensible, which must entangle the deaf mute beyond rescue in an inextricable net of uncertainty and consuming hope.

Once I saw him standing before her in the courtyard, and she was speaking at him with such violent movements of the lips and such gestures that I thought he would collapse at any moment in wild agitation.
The sweat ran down his face with the superhuman effort of grasping the sense of the hasty communication, which had been made deliberately unclear.

And the whole of the following day he lay in wait, feverish with expectation, on the dark stairs of another half sunken house that stands further along the narrow, filthy Hahnpassgasse, until he had lost the time in which he might have begged a few coppers on the corners.
And when he wanted to go home late in the evening, half dead with hunger and excitement, his foster mother had long since locked him out.
A cheerful woman’s laughter came through the wall to me from the studio next door.
Laughter? In these houses, a cheerful laugh? In the whole ghetto there lives nobody who could laugh cheerfully.

Then it occurred to me that a few days before, the old puppeteer Zwakh had confided to me that a young gentleman of quality had rented the studio from him at a high price, plainly in order to meet the chosen one of his heart without being overheard.
Little by little, every night, so that nobody in the house should notice anything, the new tenant’s costly furniture had to be carried up in secret, piece by piece.

The good natured old man had rubbed his hands with pleasure as he told me, delighted as a child at how cleverly he had managed it all: none of the other tenants could have the least notion of the romantic lovers.
And it was possible to reach the studio unnoticed from three different houses. There was even a way in through a trapdoor.
Yes, if one lifted the latch of the iron door to the loft, and that was very easy from the other side, one could come past my room to the stairs of our house and use them as a way out.

Again the cheerful laughter comes across, and it raises in me the indistinct memory of a luxurious apartment and of a noble family to whom I was often called to carry out small repairs on valuable antiques.
Suddenly I hear a shrill scream next door. I listen, startled.
The iron loft door rattles violently, and in the next moment a lady rushes into my room.
With her hair loose, white as the wall, a gold brocade thrown over her bare shoulders.
Master Pernath, hide me, for the love of Christ! Ask nothing, hide me here!
Before I could answer, my door was torn open again and at once slammed shut.
For a second the face of the junk dealer Aaron Wassertrum had grinned in like a hideous mask.
A round, shining patch rises before me, and in the light of the moon I recognise once again the foot of my bed.
Sleep still lies on me like a heavy woollen cloak, and the name Pernath stands in golden letters before my memory.
Where can I have read that name? Athanasius Pernath?
I believe, I believe that a long, long time ago I once exchanged my hat somewhere, and I wondered then that it fitted me so exactly, when I have a most peculiar shape of head.
And I looked inside the strange hat, then, and yes, yes, there it had stood in golden paper letters on the white lining:
ATHANASIUS PERNATH.
I had been wary of the hat and afraid of it, I did not know why.
Then suddenly the voice I had forgotten, the one that always wanted to know from me where the stone was that looked like fat, shoots at me like an arrow.
Quickly I picture the sharp, sickly grinning profile of red Rosina, and in this way I manage to dodge the arrow, which at once loses itself in the darkness.
Yes, Rosina’s face! That is stronger still than the dully babbling voice; and now that I shall be safe again in a moment in my room in the Hahnpassgasse, I can be quite calm.
